chapter_title: Chương 57: 0057 【Chung kết New Concept đã bắt đầu】

segments.title: Chương 57: 0057 【Chung kết New Concept đã bắt đầu】
segments.content:
The venue for the semi-finals was at the Shanghai Medical College, right next to the hotel.

The school was already on holiday, so the campus was quieter than usual, though some university students could still be seen occasionally.

The contestants in Groups A and B were all middle and high school students. They were very curious upon entering a university, looking left and right as if they were tourists.

Chen Guiliang followed his contestant number and quickly found his designated examination room and desk.

The proctors, like the registration staff from yesterday, were also past winners of the New Concept Writing Competition.

They either lived in Shanghai, or worked or studied in Shanghai, and had purely volunteered to come over and help, while also getting to know the writers.

Getting laid under false pretenses was an extremely rare behavior.

Chen Guiliang didn't recognize either of the two proctors in this examination room.

The papers were quickly handed out.

Two prompts, choose one to write an essay.

"Prompt 1: The World I Cannot Reach."

"Prompt 2: There is a very small bird that can fly for tens of thousands of miles across the Pacific Ocean. All it needs is a small twig. It holds the twig in its beak, and when it gets tired, it throws the twig onto the water's surface, then lands on it to rest for a while."

Chen Guiliang subconsciously wanted to choose the first prompt.

It was too easy to write about.

A world one wishes to reach but cannot could be a "Republic" or a "Xanadu."

A beautiful world of imagination, visible but unreachable, sought after in vain.

But Chen Guiliang stopped himself from starting.

This was a trap!

Probably 90% of the contestants this year would choose the first prompt, and their essays would all be cut from the same cloth.

But how should he write about the second prompt?

On his scratch paper, Chen Guiliang wrote down keywords like "perseverance," "fortitude," and "unyielding self-improvement."

Then he added "wisdom" and "making good use of external things."

Then he wrote "The Foolish Old Man who Moved the Mountains" and "Don Quixote."

After several minutes of consideration, Chen Guiliang found it hard to begin writing.

To write this well was far more difficult than the first prompt. A single misstep could make it cliché, or the content could end up empty and full of generalizations.

It was not an easy topic.

After thinking for a full twenty minutes, Chen Guiliang finally started to write. He directly expanded this fable into a mythological story.

The little bird was a Xuan Niao from Kunlun Mountain, but the Kunlun Celestial Palace was already in ruins, and the Queen Mother of the West was nowhere to be found. It heard that on Yingzhou, beyond the great ocean of ten thousand li, one could learn the art of becoming an immortal, so it flew across the Divine Land and the great sea.

The snows of Kunlun froze on its feathers, and the fierce astral winds tore its wings to shreds. It grabbed a withered branch and threw it onto a vast, boundless river, but when it tried to rest, it was nearly drowned by the Ruoshui River.

Legendary fairies sent it their blessings, and the Xuan Niao struggled to flap its wings, flying to the seashore. Even the Kunpeng had been stranded here, and Qiulong dragons were crying out in agony from the seabed. Black waves a hundred zhang high crashed down, causing Jiaoren to weep blood, and even mirages were shattered by the giant waves.

As he wrote, Chen Guiliang paused.

He felt the emotional impact was not strong enough; words could hardly describe that kind of celestial, fantastical world.

Moreover, the allegory wasn't deep enough.

Was it just about seeking immortality?

The Xuan Niao could be "me," seeking immortality could be "pursuing knowledge to serve the nation," and the dilapidated Kunlun Celestial Palace could be "the Chinese nation awaiting its revival."

But if written in a normal style, it could easily turn into empty slogan-shouting, reading as pompous and hollow, which would be very awkward.

What about using classical Chinese?

Or maybe write a long-form classical-style poem.

Classical-style poetry had free-form prosody, without strict requirements for tonal patterns, parallelism, or rhyme, making it very suitable to write without reference books.

Chen Guiliang immediately summarized the main points of his draft and rewrote it as a long-form classical-style poem.

He revised and edited, working on it for over an hour.

After reading it over and over, Chen Guiliang felt very satisfied, but he was afraid the judges wouldn't be able to understand it.

It was genuinely possible they wouldn't understand!

Especially some of the writers who became famous in the 80s; they were brilliant at writing in vernacular Chinese, but their foundation in classical Chinese was probably not much better than a high school student's.

It might even be worse than the high school students of today.

To put it this way, at this time, even the "Preface to the Pavilion of Prince Teng" in language textbooks had annotation errors, and very serious, commonsense ones at that, leading to the mistranslation of an entire sentence.

The textbook quoted from some reference books, and those reference books were all wrong too...

After thinking it over, there was no way he was going to change the classical poem, so he decided to write a preface for it, to help the judges understand the poem.

*In the winter of the Guiwei year, I arrived in Shanghai, and upon receiving a fable, I elaborated upon its principles.*

*It is said that in ancient times, the jingwei bird carried tiny twigs to fill the vast sea, and the Foolish Old Man chipped at stone and soil to move the great mountains. Observing the world between heaven and earth, one sees that the most minuscule can achieve the greatest of deeds, and the most simple often carries the most complex of truths.*

*Now there is a Xuan Niao, frail of body and weak of form, that beats its clipped wings, presuming to cross the great ocean, carrying a withered branch in hopes of traversing the blue waves. Its will is all the more steadfast, its actions all the more valiant...*

The two proctors were constantly walking back and forth.

When they saw an interesting essay, they would stop and stand beside the student to appreciate it carefully.

This made many contestants nervous!

Pan Yihan was a winner from the fourth competition. She lived in Shanghai and had not yet graduated from university.

She had volunteered to help proctor, wanting only to get acquainted with certain well-known writers and to become more familiar with the editors of *Mengya*.

At this moment, Pan Yihan was standing next to Chen Guiliang, looking at the essay he was copying over after finishing his revisions, already so stunned she was speechless.

Noticing that she hadn't moved for a long time, the other proctor, Gan Shijia, also walked over. Ahem, a guest writer for *iPartment 3*.

As if Chen Guiliang's essay had a paralyzing spell, Gan Shijia also suddenly stood there, motionless.

A man and a woman, the two proctors, stood by Chen Guiliang's side like left and right guardians.

It's impossible to cheat on an essay, so it didn't matter if they watched the other contestants or not. They weren't exactly neglecting their duties.

In this examination room, some people had already finished writing.

Others had put down their pens, deep in thought.

Anyone who wasn't currently writing soon noticed the proctors' strange behavior.

They guessed that this year's New Concept Writing Competition was about to produce another blockbuster essay.

At this moment, the judges were not idle either.

They were reading the outstanding essays from the preliminary round, their main job being to write comments to be printed in the collection of award-winning essays from the New Concept Writing Competition.

Comments from famous authors were a gimmick to sell the book.

This damn book had a print run of several million copies, more than the combined first-year sales of *Triple Door* and *City of Fantasy*!

Yu Hua finished reading more than ten preliminary submissions without writing a single word of commentary and casually passed them to Tie Ning beside him.

Tie Ning also had a stack of papers, which she exchanged with Yu Hua, saying with a smile, "You should at least write a few sentences."

Yu Hua said, "I'll write something when I see one that's interesting."

The ones truly frowning were the university professors, many of whom were department heads of Chinese literature. If they came across any promising talents, they might be able to offer one or two independent admission slots with reduced score requirements.

But after reviewing for half the day, the overall quality was terrible.

Worse with each passing year.

Exchanging and reviewing the essays, most of the famous authors barely put pen to paper.

They simply couldn't bring themselves to do it!

Only the writer Ma Yuan was more accommodating, commenting on seven or eight essays in one go.

Yu Hua had exchanged three batches of papers when he came across Chen Guiliang's "A Denunciation of America's Invasion of Iraq." He wanted to write a comment, but he held back.

The essay was excellent.

But it was too excellent. It didn't seem like something a high school student would write. It was highly likely written by a teacher on his behalf.

One could tell the difference between an essay by a high school student and an adult at a glance!

The depth of thought was different.

To put it this way, the overall quality of essays in Group C, which had always been overlooked by the media, far surpassed that of Groups A and B.

Because Groups A and B were for middle and high school students, while Group C was for non-students under 30 (including university students and young adults). They were only a few years older, but the things they wrote were worlds apart.

Sigh, forget it. Just treat it as getting the job done.

With strong suspicion, Yu Hua wrote a comment for Chen Guiliang's preliminary round essay.

The preliminary essays of the 200 semi-finalists were quickly reviewed by the professors and writers, but there was still a long time before the semi-final exam would end.

Due to public pressure, the competition's procedures had become more official. No one dared to casually take essays out of the examination rooms to read anymore.

A separate make-up exam was even more out of the question!

Now, all papers were collected at the same time and then delivered over together.

The professors and writers started chatting, talking idly about gossip and current affairs, and some even made plans to go for drinks.

"Old Liu, your Tsinghua University doesn't have a single slot this year?"

Cao Wenxuan, a professor from Peking University's Chinese department, asked Ge Fei, the deputy head of Tsinghua's Chinese department, out of boredom.

Ge Fei was his pen name; his real surname was Liu.

"Really, no slots. We discussed it in many meetings," Ge Fei said, shaking his head.

Cao Wenxuan sighed, "Admissions reform. It's tough for everyone."

Last year, Peking University had 150 independent admission slots, but in response to the call for reform, they had proactively reduced the number to 50.

These 50 slots were prioritized for key high schools in provinces across the country!

Cao Wenxuan had talked himself hoarse just to get one slot for the New Concept Writing Competition.

And Tsinghua?

They simply didn't give the New Concept competition any face at all, offering not a single slot.

The independent admissions at various universities were gradually returning to normal this year. But those who had been uncooperative last year were unlikely to show a better attitude this year.

Still, one had to say the right things. The head of Tsinghua's Chinese department stated: Our independent admissions this time are more biased towards science and engineering. I will report Peking University's successful experience to our university administration. We will strive to combine the New Concept Writing Competition with Tsinghua's liberal arts winter camp, treating the New Concept winners as our reserve talent pool for the liberal arts!

It was tantamount to saying nothing.

The biggest supporter was Fudan, which had given the New Concept Writing Competition five slots last year!

It was still unknown how many they would give this year.

All of the above were for admission with reduced scores, not direct admission.

The university professors walked around, probing each other, all wanting to know everyone else's situation.

The male writers, meanwhile, left in twos and threes, heading outside to smoke together under the trees.

Yu Hua was squatting, smoking and shooting the breeze, when he saw Hu Weishi hurrying over with a stack of essay papers, followed by several proctors.

"Is the exam over?" the writers asked.

Hu Weishi was all smiles, his joy even tinged with excitement. "After waiting for so many years, a truly magnificent piece of writing has finally appeared!"

Hearing this, the crowd quickly gathered around.
